ns1:channel.ns1:title: Communications Earth & Environment
ns1:channel.ns1:description:
Communications Earth & Environment is an open access journal from Nature Portfolio that publishes high-quality research, reviews and commentary in the Earth, environmental and planetary sciences. The papers we publish represent significant advances that bring new insight to a specialized area of research. We also provide a community forum for issues of importance to Earth, environmental and planetary scientists, regardless of sub-discipline.

Our scope covers all areas of the geosciences, climate and environmental sciences as well as planetary sciences, including those at the interface with ecology, sustainability and environmental social sciences. Primary research of interest to the journal includes important insights gained from field work, novel analyses of existing data, numerical or analytical modelling, theoretical studies or laboratory experiments.

We encourage submissions that provide independent confirmation of particularly influential publications.

The submission and review processes are managed by our in-house professional editors supported by our Editorial Board Members, who provide technical expertise across the breadth of the Earth, environmental and planetary sciences. We are committed to rapid dissemination of important research results. Articles are published on a continuous basis to ensure swift communication of findings.

ns1:item.ns1:title: Attribution estimates for similar extremes are robust across event definitions
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04053-2

Comparable attribution methods yield consistent results despite sensitivity to event definitions, while dataset choice has the largest influence on attribution statements, even in regions with dense and high-quality observations.
ns1:item.dc:title: Attribution estimates for similar extremes are robust across event definitions

ns1:item.ns1:title: Inundation risk in North China’s coastal gateway amid land subsidence, sea-level rise and coastal defense initiatives
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04068-9

By 2100, IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) reported relative sea level rise may erase 373 to 458 square kilometers in the Bohai Economic Rim, with local land subsidence increasing losses by 110 to 260 percent; levees reduce flooding and population exposure, according to satellite radar, sea level rise, and demographic projections

ns1:item.ns1:title: Wildfire synchronicity across European regions is favored by specific weather regimes
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-03956-4

Synchronous wildfires in Europe are favored by weather regimes that promote warm, dry, and sometimes windy meteorological anomalies, such as the Atlantic Ridge in summer and European Blocking in spring, as revealed by satellite wildfire observations and atmospheric reanalysis.
ns1:item.dc:title: Wildfire synchronicity across European regions is favored by specific weather regimes

ns1:item.ns1:title: Subdued surface expression of deep cave collapse
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04016-7

Kilometer-scale linear depressions on Australia’s Nullarbor Plain record collapse and sagging above deep cave conduits, providing criteria for recognizing otherwise subdued cave-collapse systems, according to morphometrics, geophysics, cave records, cliff exposures and sedimentology analyses.
ns1:item.dc:title: Subdued surface expression of deep cave collapse

ns1:item.ns1:title: Coupled orbital and sea-level forcing on the Pacific Walker Circulation during the past 800 kyrs
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04062-1

The split Pacific Walker Circulation shows periodic variation through the geological past, with El Niño Modoki patterns favored during glacial periods and La Niña Modoki patterns favored during interglacial periods after 250 ka, according to the reconstructed ENSO Modoki Index over the past 800,000 years.
ns1:item.dc:title: Coupled orbital and sea-level forcing on the Pacific Walker Circulation during the past 800 kyrs
